activities.title: Semantic Quantization in KV Cache Eviction
activities.description:
When a program runs out of memory, the operating system does not crash, it uses a page replacement policy to swap pages in and out, keeping the most useful ones active.

LLMs processing long texts face a similar memory bottleneck. They store a "KV cache" (memory buffer) that grows linearly with sequence length. At 32,000 tokens, this cache requires ~11.6 GB of VRAM. If you try to run this on a standard 8 GB GPU, the process runs out of memory and crashes.

Popular open-source solutions like H2O and SnapKV try to evict less important tokens using attention weights. However, calculating these weights across long contexts creates an even larger memory bottleneck, causing OOM crashes anyway.

I built EntropyKV to solve this using systems design principles rather than complex ML overhead. EntropyKV operates like an OS page replacement policy for model memory:

Result: EntropyKV cuts cache memory by 43% (11.6 GB → 6.6 GB) and speeds up generation by 32×, allowing long-context models to run on standard 8 GB consumer GPUs where competing methods crash.

Crucially, when cache space is cut by 50%, the model doesn't output garbage. It exhibits what we call "semantic quantization" : it perfectly preserves the structure and meaning of the retrieved context while only losing fine numeric details (e.g., retrieving "2023" instead of "2026").
keyTakeaways: Understand why traditional attention-based KV cache eviction methods fail (OOM) at long contexts on consumer GPUs.
Learn how to implement a lightweight, attention-free eviction policy using only key and value vector norms.
Explore how layer-adaptive allocation (LARA) acts as a tiered caching strategy across different layers of a model.
Witness the "semantic quantization" effect, showing how neural networks gracefully degrade like JPEGs under lossy memory compression.

activities.title: Databases in Ethereum Nodes
activities.description:
General-purpose databases handle the overwhelming majority of workloads. Pick a flavor — relational, NoSQL, column-store, in-memory — tune its config, and it'll fit an enormous range of problems.

But in some fields, we need to go down to the fundamentals and build a custom database from the ground up. In bioinformatics, the need is often to store petabytes of data and/or have a database that can efficiently do string operations on structures like suffix trees or the Burrows–Wheeler Transform (FM-index). Blockchains are another such field. They work under different constraints — unique access patterns, authenticated state for a trustless environment, distribution requirements and different artifacts to store.

The Ethereum Foundation coordinates with a cohort of client teams that drive protocol research and development. Pretty much every client has come up with custom storage solutions. Erigon is one of these client teams; it specializes in archive nodes — the biggest node type by storage size, relied on by node/RPC providers (Infura, Alchemy, QuickNode) and by indexers and analytics platforms (The Graph, Dune, Etherscan).

In this session, I will talk about ErigonDB, the custom database devised by Erigon. It's a multi-tiered database with an mmap'd B-tree (MDBX) at L0 and custom snapshots at the lower levels. It provides transactional semantics, and the immutable snapshots are distributed via torrent to other nodes. We'll explore the data model, succinct data structures, custom file formats and algorithms that power ErigonDB — and of course the constraints and motivations that drove those decisions.
keyTakeaways: access patterns in blockchains in general and ethereum in particular
kinds of data that need to be stored in an ethereum node and the distribution requirements
the architecture of the custom database; composing ACID properties
different algorithms and data structures used in database - recsplit, elias-fano, existence filters, good old btree and so on.

activities.title: From HIDL to Stable AIDL: Modernizing Android HAL Interfaces
activities.description: Android is transitioning from HIDL to Stable AIDL to improve HAL interface stability and long-term maintainability. However, many production devices still depend on legacy HIDL implementations, making upgrades difficult.This talk presents a migration of a HAL from HIDL to Stable AIDL, focusing on real-world challenges. It covers key differences in interface definition, versioning, Binder IPC, and VINTF compatibility. The session walks through a step-by-step migration: rewriting interfaces, updating services, and modifying manifests.Hands-on guide for engineers who must modernize existing HIDL HALs to Stable AIDL in shipping devices.
keyTakeaways: Explain the core architectural differences between HIDL and AIDL in the Android HAL stack.
List the Android version milestones that make AIDL mandatory for new and production devices.
Execute a step-by-step HIDL → AIDL migration for a real hardware interface.
Address SELinux policy changes, VINTF manifest updates, and compatibility matrix versioning required by the migration.
Identify and mitigate common failure, validation.

People interested in FOSS-based enterprises and who are looking to learn and discuss about alternative enterprise forms

activities.title: FOSS in the Public Consciousness
activities.description:
This is inspired by @Muneer_S’s thread on how to engage the average citizen to care about FOSS.

To paraphrase the linked discussion: we have numerous FOSS events, and while they have their purpose, a lot of them are “preaching to the converted” in the sense that they are limited in getting more people to learn about FOSS. If you look at the reach of such meetups and conference outside tech circles, this reach plummets to nearly zero.

We need to think of ways to spread awareness about FOSS to people outside tech circles. Often, this could start with simply making people aware about better alternatives for the services they use—whether that “better” means ad-free, using less resources, or other practical benefits. This could be creators realising their platform of choice is slowly locking them down and squeezing their assets; small business having a niggling feeling that the data they share in benefiting platforms more than the platforms are benefitting them; or simply people thinking they’ve been asked to share their phone number in one place too many.

On the other hand, there are groups of people who share similar ideas to to FOSS (and the Free Software movement especially) such as wanting things to be run by the community in an open way and with people having a say, but they may not know how to apply this to software. One example at the institutional level: NGOs or research institutes collecting research data meant for the public good, but using proprietary software which causes the data to be locked down into proprietary formats.

How does one spread awareness of FOSS outside of tech circles?

One idea I had was to go and give talks about FOSS related topics in non-tech events and aimed at a non-tech audience. Other ideas included creating social media graphics and videos, advertising on buses and in metro stations, and sitting and interacting with people in public spaces (such as Church Street in Bangalore).

Coming up with more such ideas and turning them into concrete action points is, in essence, the agenda of this BoF.

These can be fine-tuned later based on feedback or live based on how the discussion progresses, but this would be the general idea.

An introduction to set the context, followed by a round-table discussion. We will leave a few minutes open at the end for free-flowing discussion and to exchange contacts in case people want to take this beyond the BoF and coordinate further.

activities.title: Navigating the FOSS Contribution Journey
activities.description:
Many developers see open source as a destination: get your first pull request merged, participate in Hacktoberfest, maybe even crack Google Summer of Code. But in reality, open source is a journey - one that evolves from curiosity to contribution, from contribution to ownership, and from ownership to leadership.

In this talk, I will share my unconventional path through the FOSS ecosystem. What started as participation in FOSS Hack (India's largest open-source hackathon) eventually led to building and maintaining projects used by thousands of developers, and growing it into an official Google Summer of Code organization, mentoring contributors worldwide.

Through stories of first contributions, rejected pull requests, community building, mentorship, and project stewardship, this session will explore what it really takes to grow in open source. We'll discuss how contributors can find projects they genuinely care about, navigate complex codebases, build credibility within communities, and transition from being "someone who contributes" to someone who creates opportunities for others.

We will also cover how contributing to large-scale industry led open source projects requires a slightly different approach.

Whether you're wondering how to make your first contribution or thinking about becoming a maintainer, this talk offers practical lessons, hard-earned insights, and a roadmap for building a meaningful and sustainable open-source journey.
keyTakeaways: A practical roadmap for getting started in FOSS.
How documentation, testing, design, community support, and issue triage are also valuable entry points into open source.
How long-term contributions come from genuine interest and alignment with a project's mission and community.
Open source is a people-first ecosystem where communication, collaboration, and empathy often have a bigger impact than technical expertise alone.
How consistent participation can lead to maintainer responsibilities, mentorship opportunities, and leadership roles.
How to evolve projects that begin as weekend experiments into thriving open-source communities with global contributors.
Lessons on growing from contributor to maintainer and the required skills.
Insights into building and sustaining open-source communities.
and more..

activities.title: Bend, don't Break. Modern Techniques for Flexibility in Strongly Typed Functional Programming
activities.description:
Strong static guarantees of runtime behaviour, and fighting the compiler until it and you come to a shared mutual understanding. If these two things usually go hand in hand for you, then this talk is for you!

This talk is at its core, a compendium of the techniques that functional programmers employ to keep programming pleasant without losing any of the safety and robustness. It’s not really about advanced type systems (we will never mention dependent types, promise), but it is about bending the type system to your will, and that, predictably, requires gaining some understanding of a few slightly advanced type systems topics. While we will provide a brief overview of everything, familiarity with Haskell, PureScript, OCaml, Rust, Lean, or some other statically typed programming language is recommended.

Some things we will look at and how to apply them to real world code -- Establishing invariants, convincing the compiler to relax the inbuilt checks because you took care of them already- Producing, consuming, and traversing dynamic values of unknown structure, sealing structures so the compiler knows safety is preserved- Building extensible data structures and extensible algorithms. Performing type safe dynamic dispatch and dependency injection
keyTakeaways: Flexibility and type safety are not a trade-off. You will learn how to get both in modern functional languages.
Advanced types are a tool to improve your development experience, not to engage in type astronomy. You will learn how advanced types make it easier to read and write code.
Learn how to guide the compiler effectively so that it shifts your relationship with the compiler from a battle into a cooperative partnership.

activities.title: Living With a DeGoogled Phone: Privacy, Trade-offs, and Daily Use
activities.description:
Many Android phones come with heavy vendor skins and a lot of Google services built in. I wanted something lighter and more private, so I moved from that setup to a custom ROM with less Google dependence.

That shift was not smooth. I ran into soft bricks, a hard brick, SafetyNet and Play Integrity problems, and notifications that did not always behave the way they should. I also tried microG, but in the end I went with a fully vanilla custom ROM setup because that fit my privacy goals better. Along the way, I managed to fix most of the issues I ran into, but a few things never really had a clean or satisfying fix.

For family devices, though, a fully degoogled setup did not make sense. They needed something that was easier to live with, so those phones stayed on a normal GApps-based custom ROM. That ended up being one of the biggest lessons for me: the same setup that feels fine for one person can be too much trouble for someone else.

This talk is about that move, the things that broke along the way, the fixes that worked, the things that stayed broken, and the trade-offs between privacy and daily use.

activities.title: Volume Controller using Knob (Potentiometer)

Building a Physical Volume Knob for AOSP on Raspberry Pi 5

In this talk, I'll show how I connected a rotary potentiometer to a Raspberry Pi 5 running AOSP Android 15 and made it control the media volume — using a 250-line C++ daemon in the vendor layer, with zero changes to the Android framework.

Along the way we hit real walls: a library blocked by VNDK, build and runtime errors, three SELinux types that don't exist in AOSP 15, and a hardware bus number that wasn't what we expected.

How to read hardware sensors from a native C++ daemon using standard Linux kernel ABIs
How uinput works and why it is sometimes the right way to talk to Android audio from vendor code

The difference between BOARD_VENDOR_SEPOLICY_DIRS and PRODUCT_PRIVATE_SEPOLICY_DIRS and why it matters

activities.title: PeerDAS: Erasure Coding When You Can't Trust the Storage
activities.description:
You've probably used erasure coding without calling it that. RAID, CDs that still play with scratches on them, most distributed storage systems. The idea is you add redundancy up front so you can lose some of the data and still rebuild it. Reed-Solomon is the usual workhorse, and the property you care about is that any ~50% of the encoded pieces is enough to get everything back.

The catch is that all of those systems assume the storage isn't out to get you. A disk can die, but it won't deliberately hand you corrupted bytes, and it won't sit on the exact pieces you need while pretending everything's fine. Once the thing storing your data is an untrusted peer who might be malicious, that assumption is gone, and plain erasure coding isn't enough anymore.

This talk is about what you have to add to make it work anyway. I'll use PeerDAS as the example because it shipped on a live Ethereum network in December 2025, and several independent open-source clients had to implement the same protocol and actually interoperate.

I'll cover why a malicious peer is harder than a failing disk, specifically the two separate problems: it can serve you wrong data, or it can withhold the pieces you're missing. Those need different solutions. For the first, KZG commitments let you check that a single chunk is the real thing without downloading the whole dataset. For the second, you sample a handful of random chunks, and because of the erasure coding, that's enough to be confident the whole thing is really available. Then there's the networking layer: deciding who stores which pieces, passing samples around between peers, and letting the network reconstruct data that's gone missing.

This talk would be nothing about blockchain. Just a genuinely hard distributed systems problem and how people solved it.
keyTakeaways: what erasure coding gives you and why that 50% reconstruction number is the thing that makes the whole approach possible
why storage that fails is a different problem from storage that lies, and why one set of tricks doesn't cover both
how you check a small chunk is correct without pulling down the dataset it came from
the basic idea of data availability sampling: look at a few random pieces, conclude something about all of them
how the network actually spreads the data out, shares samples, and repairs itself, and a couple of the practical tradeoffs that came with shipping it

activities.title: How FOSS and AI are Changing Government Workflows at NHAI
activities.description:
In 2025, IndiaFOSS was the first in-person developer event I ever attended. Right after returning to Delhi, I joined the AI Cell at NHAI, the National Highways Authority of India. So it is kind of a full circle moment as a year later, after a lot of trial and error, this talk is supposed to be a reflection on what we have been able to build, what surprised us, and what FOSS made possible inside a public-sector organization.

Government organizations are often assumed to be slow adopters of new technology, and for good reason, their structure has those constraints and inertia to make them so. At the same time, outside of coding tools, enterprise AI adoption for knowledge work products has been slow, shallow, or stuck at the demo stage.

Our experience at NHAI has complicated both assumptions.

With a small team of designers and engineers, working closely with NHAI insiders, we have been able to build a set of internal AI and productivity tools for the organization.

Marg Sarthi, NHAI’s internal AI assistant, is the flagship example. In production, it has crossed 15,000+ conversations, 50,000+ questions being asked by 1,000+ internal NHAI employees, with 2 out of 3 being repeat users coming back at least once a week.

That gave us a chance to ask why this worked as a daily workflow tool when many internal AI assistants struggle to gain their footing beyond demos. People use it not as a generic chat interface, but for work they already do: finding policy circulars, interpreting clauses, drafting notes and letters, querying project data, working with scanned data heavy PDFs, and navigating approval-heavy processes.

Along with this, across NH-AI, we have built smaller tools as well, from document utilities to workflow-specific assistants. A pattern that we see emerging: each useful tool had builders on one side and an organizational counterpart on the other who pushed for these tools and iterated with us quickly. These institutional co-creators helped translate messy internal needs into product direction: what users would trust, what workflows mattered, and where governance boundaries could not be hand-waved away.

FOSS has mattered tremendously in us being able to make this possible, because it gave this small team agency, often rare in a process led traditional organization. In a closed vendor-led setup, every meaningful change can become a request: wait for procurement, wait for roadmap alignment, wait for customization, wait for integration support. In our case, the ability to run, inspect, adapt, and extend open systems meant that user feedback could turn into working software quickly.

One particular OSS - LibreChat became the base of a tool like Margsarthi and gave us a hackable foundation for the assistant along with MCP giving us a way to connect tools and data without rebuilding the whole chat layer. Forgejo and self-hostable observability tools helped us keep ownership of the development and feedback loop.

This led to us working with proven primitives and being able to ship faster. AI has made this even more powerful. A small team could understand unfamiliar open-source codebases faster, customize them around our workflows, and build tools that would have been too slow to attempt if every change depended on an external vendor cycle.

We do not think that we have a final playbook for government AI, but we have arrived at hints of it as we do have a real production story from inside one public institution: how FOSS and AI helped us move faster, customize deeper, avoid vendor-roadmap bottlenecks, and build tools close enough to daily work that people actually used them.

This talk shares what we learned from that journey, and why the future of AI in government may depend as much on open infrastructure and institutional co-creators as it does on base models.
keyTakeaways: One lesson from this work is that adoption is often a timing problem. In large organizations, the need may be real, but by the time a vendor cycle, procurement loop, or customization request produces something usable, the workflow has shifted or users have already found a workaround.

We want attendees to see how FOSS changes that loop: not just by reducing cost, but by giving institutions the ability to inspect, adapt, host, observe, and replace the systems they depend on. Because the team could build on open, extensible systems and stay close to NHAI stakeholders, feedback could turn into working software quickly enough for users to try it in their daily workflows.

The talk will also cover why internal co-creators matter. NHAI insiders helped translate organizational needs, trust concerns, and governance boundaries into product direction, so the tools were not just technically possible but institutionally usable.

Finally, we want to make the case for internal AI capacity in government. Vendors can be useful, but transformation cannot be fully outsourced. When a small internal team of designers and engineers works with institutional co-creators and owns enough of the stack, it can adapt faster, learn from users directly, and build systems that are accountable to the organization rather than only delivered to it.

activities.title: Under the Hood of Android , What Really Happens When You Open an App?
activities.description: Have you ever stopped to think about what actually happens inside your smartphone the second you tap an app icon? Instead of booting up from scratch every single time , our phone uses a shortcut to clone a ready to go template which is why our apps launch in the blink of an eye.We build apps every day , many complex ones as well relying on APIs that make UI magically appear but how many of us actually understand the heavy lifting happening underneath? This talk will cover that black box of Android’s operating system for developers who want to look past the surface layer. Did you know that the app doesn’t boot a fresh JVM every time but instead forks from a pre warmed Zygote process to launch instantly. Most importantly, because this entire operating system is open - source , you never have to just guess how things work , we can actually read the blueprints. I’ll show you how to navigate this massive public codebase so you can look up exactly what happens under the hood whenever you get stuck
keyTakeaways: Understand the Zygote forking model and why Android app startup is fast
Know the journey from tapping an icon -> process creation -> first frame on screen
Understand how Compose's compiler plugin + slot table architecture differs from the legacy View system

activities.title: Benchmarking can be hard, here's why we're still creating a new one for OCaml
activities.description: Software and hardware are continuously evolving. New innovations & improvements help bring us better performance gains and sometimes things work out like magic. This is also true for programming languages like Java and OCaml. And yet, while developing our research ideas and trying to argue about performance, its hard to comprehend what we’re seeing: Is my benchmark now faster because of what we did, or was it another previous unrelated change showing up now? Is it better caching or was it the garbage collector being triggered? How can we be sure. There is, thus, a need to get reliable feedback while building up our systems and often benchmark suites can be key in guiding us.In this talk, we’ll try to visualize how benchmarking can be hard, what to look out for and with helpful scenarios all along the way. We will briefly look into how this may show up in real life in the context of improving OCaml: an industrial strength functional programming language. Finally, we describe some of the ideas, old & new, we’re thinking about to help us grow, quantify, and maintain(!) a new benchmark suite to aid us in bringing more cutting edge research to our users without sacrificing on legacy code nor slowing down production workloads.
keyTakeaways: Why do we care about benchmarks while developing and why these can be hard
Ways to build reliable feedback from benchmarks and maintaining them as systems grow
A quick intro to OCaml that hopefully piques your interest to learn about it more :)

activities.title: Rust in Android: Building Secure HALs for the Next Generation of AOSP
activities.description:
As Android continues adopting Rust to improve security and reliability, platform developers are gaining new ways to build safer system components. This talk introduces Android Hardware Abstraction Layers (HALs) developed using Rust and AIDL, covering how Rust integrates with AOSP, Binder IPC, and modern Android architecture.

Through a practical example, attendees will learn how to create and integrate a Rust-based HAL, understand the benefits of memory safety, and explore why Rust is becoming an important part of Android's future.
keyTakeaways: Understand why Android is adopting Rust for system-level development.
Explain how AIDL-based HALs fit into the modern Android architecture.
Create and integrate a Rust-based HAL in AOSP.
Implement Binder IPC communication between Android services and Rust HALs.
Identify common challenges when developing and debugging Rust HAL services.

activities.title: Building OpenSpeaks tools for language documentation and archiving
activities.description:

activities.title: Offline-first mobile apps on Frappe: a metadata-driven Flutter SDK with server-side control
activities.description:
Frappe keeps everything about a form on the server. The fields, the validations, the workflow, and the permissions all live in the DocType and change whenever someone edits it. A mobile app that copies that structure into hardcoded screens breaks the day a DocType gets a new field. To fix it you ship a new build to the Play Store, and a field worker on a weak connection may never download it. Add poor or missing network, where the app has to collect data offline and reconcile it later against a server that has also changed, and building mobile on Frappe gets hard fast. This talk is about how we made it tractable, and the code is open source.

We built two pieces that sit on top of Frappe core.

frappe-mobile-control is a Frappe app in Python (AGPL-3.0). It runs on your existing server and decides what the mobile app may do: which DocTypes appear on the phone and in what order, the minimum app version a user must have, whether the app is in maintenance mode, and how login works (password, mobile OTP, or OAuth with PKCE, with token refresh). You change any of this from Frappe Desk and the phone picks it up on the next sync.

frappe-mobile-sdk is a Flutter package in Dart (MIT). Give it a Frappe site and a config file and it builds a working app. It reads the DocType metadata and renders the form for you, with more than twenty field types including links, child tables, and geolocation. It handles the REST calls, the workflow actions, and role permissions, and it stores data in a local SQLite database that syncs both ways.

Four layers, one sync channel. The server stays the source of truth; the SDK renders forms from metadata and works offline; you build only your own UI and logic.

Offline is the focus of the talk. It is easy to describe and full of sharp edges once real users and real networks show up. What we had to solve, and how:

Collect with no network, survive an interrupted sync, and handle a record edited in two places: resumable cursor, conflict guard, dependency-ordered sync, write-ahead logging with serialized writes, a background isolate, and encryption at rest.

A pull that gets killed halfway on a weak connection should not start over. We save the sync position in SQLite so it resumes from where it stopped.

When a phone uploads a record at the same moment the server sends down a newer copy, the two can clash. We added a guard so neither one silently overwrites the other.

Records often depend on each other: a parent and its child rows, or a record and its attachment. We sync them in order and upload attachments first, so you never store a row that points at a file that is not there yet.

SQLite used to crash when several writes arrived together. We turned on write-ahead logging, made writes happen one at a time, and moved sync onto a separate Dart isolate so the screen never freezes while data moves.

When someone adds a field on the server while a form is open on the phone, the app keeps a fingerprint of the form's structure, notices its copy is stale, and refreshes before saving instead of crashing or dropping the field.

The local database is encrypted on the device, because in our work it holds personal data like Aadhaar numbers that should not sit in plain text on a phone in the field.

A field added on the server, with no app rebuild. The old hardcoded app threw NoSuchFieldError; this one picks the field up on the next sync.

We will demo all of this on a real device, not on slides. We build an app from a config file, add a field on the server and watch it appear after a restart with no new build, put the phone in airplane mode and collect a few records, then come back online and watch them sync. We kill the app mid-sync to show it resume, and edit a record on the server while the phone is offline to show how the conflict is handled.

This is not a prototype. The SDK already runs in production apps that field teams use to collect data for large social-sector programmes, on real phones, in places with little or no connectivity. The demo is the same code those teams run.

Both repositories are open. You can install the server app with bench, pull the SDK from pub.dev, point it at your own Frappe site, and build on it or send a patch.
keyTakeaways: How to drive a mobile app's forms, permissions, and versioning from the Frappe server, so a schema change does not need a new app build.
How to render Frappe DocType forms dynamically in Flutter, including links, child tables, and geolocation, without writing the screens by hand.
How an offline sync engine behaves in the field: resuming an interrupted pull, ordering records that depend on each other, and handling a record edited in two places.
Practical ways to keep offline SQLite stable and safe on a field device: write-ahead logging, one-at-a-time writes, a background sync thread, and on-device encryption.
Where to get the code (MIT SDK on pub.dev, AGPL-3.0 server app) and how to build on it or contribute.

activities.title: What LLVM Does Differently When The Target Is CPU VS GPU
activities.description:
Most people working with LLVM know the pipeline: source → IR → analysis passes → optimization passes → codegen to machine code. What's less obvious is that when learning about this pipeline, they silently assume the target is a CPU, but LLVM lowers and optimizes for GPUs too.

In this talk I'll take a function, compile it for x86-64 and NVPTX, and walk through exactly where the pipelines diverge and why. We'll see what the middle-end shares between the two targets and where things change fundamentally. I will also cover the instruction selection differences between the two-level ISA on NVIDIA (PTX → SASS) vs direct ISA emission on AMD.

The talk closes with a look at LLVM's growing role in GPU development with projects like cuTile and CUDA-OXIDE both targeting LLVM IR and why that makes LLVM contribution directly relevant to the future of open GPU tooling.

activities.title: Launcher3 Internals: Understanding Android's Home Screen, Google Feed Integration, and Custom -1 Panels
activities.description:
Launcher3 is one of the most frequently used yet least understood applications in the Android ecosystem. Every interaction on an Android device eventually flows through it, unlocking the device, launching applications, accessing widgets, navigating recent tasks, searching for content, or interacting with personalized experiences such as Google Feed.

Over the last year, while maintaining and customizing Launcher3 across multiple Android releases, I repeatedly dived into parts of the launcher that are rarely documented and even less frequently discussed in public. It started from writing features and maintenance and swiftly became a deep exploration into Launcher3's architecture, integration, plugin overlays, feed provider, the mechanism that power the familiar -1 screen experience found on millions of Android devices.

Many Android developers work on Launcher3, but few get the opportunity to understand why it is structured the way it is. This talk aims to bridge that gap.

Launcher3 is not just an app that opens other apps. It is one of the central part of the Android experience, such as navigation, recents, search, widgets and personalisation. This session will cover its core architecture, workspace, states, and integration with SystemUI. We will also examine how OEMs and custom ROMs extend the same codebase to create different launcher experiences

A major focus of the session will be understanding the architecture behind the Google Feed (-1) screen. Through practical examples and analysis, we will explore how overlay provider plugin communicate with Launcher3, how overlay services are implemented, and what developers can learn when building their own custom launcher experiences.

Along the way, I will also share real-world lessons learned from maintaining Launcher3 customizations, debugging launcher issues across Android releases, and studying the components that make modern Android launchers feel seamless to users.

Whether you maintain a custom ROM, work on the Android platform, or are simply interested in how Android launchers work, this session will help you understand how Launcher3 is structured, how its major components interact, and how modern launcher features are implemented.
keyTakeaways: Understand how Launcher3 evolved from a simple application launcher into a core component of the modern Android user experience.
Learn how Launcher3 interacts with SystemUI, Recents, Search, and many more platform services.
Explore the architecture behind Google Feed and the implementation of Android's -1 screen experience.
Understand launcher overlay plugins and other mechanisms used by libgooglefeed.
Learn practical techniques for customizing Launcher3 and implementing alternative feed experiences.
Gain insights for Launcher3 maintenance, debugging, and reverse-engineering efforts across Android releases.
Walk away with a mental model of Launcher3 that makes future customization and platform development significantly easier.

activities.title: PythonBPF - now with loops, custom funcs, and more maps!
activities.description:
PythonBPF is a project that enables developers to write eBPF programs in pure Python, essentially allowing you to write code that runs inside your kernel in Python.

We allow a reduced Python grammar to be used for the eBPF-specific parts of code. This allows users to:

Feel free to go through the project's README to get an overview of how this is done.

Our goal with this session is to explain how some parts of PythonBPF work, as well as gain insight into what new features that people who might use PythonBPF need.

We’ll briefly discuss what PythonBPF is (for the uninitiated), how it overcomes the shortcomings of other ways of writing eBPF code, and what’s new in PythonBPF since it was last demoed at FOSDEM - loops, custom functions, a better type deduction system and support for more helpers

Why PythonBPF is needed.
New features we recently added to PythonBPF and why you might want to try it out
A request for community help in development

activities.title: Bypassing Android MTP: pushing a native C++ daemon via ADB for fast storage analysis
activities.description:
We all have been through this tough battle at least once in our lives with MTP (Media Transfer Protocol), which is what every OS uses when you plug an Android phone in via USB. It was designed in 2008 for portable media players and transfers file metadata one item at a time with no caching or parallel requests. It does a round trip every time new info is needed because it works as a request-response protocol, so when you club this with modern tech with 100s of GBs of storage and tens of thousands of files, even calculating folder sizes takes several minutes, and if you are on macOS, the Finder app doesn't even show folder sizes at all. SocketSweep is an open source desktop app that bypasses this agonising MTP entirely. The main source of architectural inspiration is the scrcpy project by Genymobile, the idea of pushing a native binary to an Android device via ADB and communicating over a local socket.

So here's how it works: we have a cross-compiled C++ daemon (~1MB static binary, built with the Android NDK for aarch64) that gets pushed to the phone via adb push. Now the transferred daemon binds to a TCP socket on port 5050 and scans the filesystem using native POSIX calls like opendir/readdir/stat directly on the device, so there's no MTP bottleneck, it's plain raw system calls. Now the ADB port forwarding tunnels TCP 5050 on the phone to localhost:5050 on the PC, giving us a reliable bidirectional channel through the USB cable (with future scope of making it work over WiFi). Coming to the desktop side, we have a Rust/Tauri backend on the PC which manages the full lifecycle from pushing the daemon, setting up port forwarding, handling scoped storage permissions, and managing the TCP connection. The app uses a React frontend with an interactive treemap visualization.

A full /sdcard scan on my device, which is a Samsung S24 Ultra (256GB, ~47k files), took about 7 seconds.

In this lightning talk i'll walk through why MTP is slow at the protocol level, how the "push binary + socket" pattern from scrcpy can be applied to other problems, cross-compiling C++ for Android with the NDK, and how ADB port forwarding works as a communication layer.
keyTakeaways: Why MTP is slow at the protocol level and why building better file manager apps on top of it doesn't fix the core problem
How scrcpy's "push a native binary via ADB, communicate over a local socket" pattern can be reused to build your own Android tools
A working example of this pattern: scanning 47k files in ~7 seconds vs several minutes over MTP
Why this approach is future-proof: it runs through ADB debugging, not sideloading, so it continues to work even as Google tightens sideloading restrictions on Android

activities.title: LGTM Is Not A Theorem
activities.description:
My time at IBM, MathWorks, and AWS prior to my PhD taught me that software engineering principles are adaptable guidelines, not rigid laws. MathWorks demanded an exceptionally high bar for rigorous testing because its software simulates safety-critical systems. Conversely, AWS prioritized a first-mover advantage, driving rapid delivery. Ultimately, an organization’s testing bandwidth depends on whether the business goal is immaculate quality or speed-to- market. Navigating these philosophies means as an engineer you need to align yourself with a company’s operational reality and adapting to the business demand.

Is formal verification overrated? No. However, it is economically unfeasible if treated as an all-or-nothing pursuit of total correctness. This talk argues for a pragmatic middle ground: proving what we can, where it matters most. Moving up the assurance ladder shouldn’t require verifying an entire software stack. In a typical production setup, like a Django web server talking to a database, verifying the Python-to-JSON translation or the FFI is largely intractable. Instead, the buck stops at the interface. I show how to use formal methods to ensure core application contracts strictly abide by the expected specification, bypassing the messy infrastructure. We aren’t proving the universe; we just want to verify the critical layers in between.
keyTakeaways: The audience will walk away with a clear design mindset. This pivots the software engineering discussion away from endless code generation and toward the economics of formal properties. Instead of chasing the expensive illusion of total correctness, attendees will learn to target resources effectively at critical interface layers. Ultimately, this approach forces us to evaluate a vital question: does our target theorem represent a strong, structural property, or just a weak, superficial one?

activities.title: Open Code, Curated Data: Building Open Water Intelligence for Indian Cities
activities.description:
Neer Vazhvu (neervazhvu.org) is an open-source platform that turns scattered public water data into living, interactive maps. It is live across three Indian cities (Chennai, Madurai and Bengaluru), with a fourth, Mumbai, in progress, built by a very small team.

The starting problem: a city's water data sits in many separate silos, across different departments, portals, and formats, so no one sees the whole picture and the warning signs get missed.

The heart of the talk is architecture: how we serve several cities from one codebase. A new city is mostly configuration, data, and capability flags rather than a forked codebase, and I will be honest about where that discipline holds and where it leaks.

How the system is designed for partners to contribute data without us as the bottleneck: fixed layer contracts plus ingest and validation scripts, so onboarding a new river basin is meant to be a manifest and a data drop rather than a rewrite.

The data pipelines: parsing government PDFs, portals, and satellite imagery into standardized, provenance-tagged layers.

The honest part: the code is the easy bit. Curated, maintained, trustworthy data is the hard one. I will cover what "open" really means here, why open source and open data are different problems, and the open question of how a civic project stays both open and sustainable.

A live demo across the cities.
keyTakeaways: A reusable pattern for building multi-city civic platforms from one codebase, using configuration and capability flags instead of forking.
A clear-eyed distinction between open source and open data, and what each means for a public-interest project.
A realistic picture of what it takes to sustain open civic infrastructure with a very small team and almost no budget.

activities.title: Physics at 60FPS
activities.description: Rapier is the Rust ecosystem’s flagship physics engine: one codebase that ships 2D and 3D, f32 and f64, native and WebAssembly, with optional cross-platform determinism and full state snapshots. This talk uses a live, walkable browser world (built with Runek, a procedural 3D component registry) as the demo, then digs into what Rapier does right as a Rust project: arena-and-handle API design, structure-of-arrays data layout, a clean WASM boundary, and feature-flagged determinism. We’ll compare it honestly against Avian, Jolt, PhysX, and the JS incumbents, and pull out lessons for any Rust crate that targets WASM.

activities.title: Zero Trust, Zero TEE: Porting Android 16 to a Device Whose Security Stack Doesn't Exist Yet
activities.description:
Android's security model is a chain of promises. Bootloader trusts TrustZone. TrustZone backs HWKM. HWKM feeds Keystore2. Keystore2 trusts VINTF manifests. Every security writeup, every hardening guide, every architecture diagram assumes this chain is intact and working.

Bring-up doesn't get that luxury. Bring-up starts from nothing. This talk is about porting YAAP (Android 16/17) to the Motorola Vienna (MT6878, Dimensity 6300) and watching Android's security stack fail to assemble itself - in three specific, revealing ways.

Failure 1 - The Silent Boot Loop

inlinecrypt in fstab tells the kernel to use inline hardware encryption

The key lives inside a Trustonic TA inside TrustZone - which isn't initialized yet during early bring-up

The kernel just waits. No panic. No log entry. Absolute silence.

What this exposes: the kernel-TEE dependency is far tighter than anything in the framework-level docs suggests

Failure 2 - The VINTF Lie

The vendor blob dump shipped with Thales StrongBox VINTF declarations intact

StrongBox wasn't actually there. The manifest said it was.

Keystore2 believed the manifest. Watchdog crashes started firing.

What this exposes: VINTF is a contract, and when the vendor side of that contract is wrong, the framework has no graceful fallback - it just breaks

Failure 3 - The Upstream Bug

A casing inconsistency in libwifi_hal/Android.bp in AOSP 17 silently killed the WiFi HAL

Not a vendor issue. A bug in mainline AOSP itself.

Debug path: logcat -> VINTF resolution failure -> build system trace -> the single wrong-case character in Android.bp

The security angle most bring-up talks never touch:

When Keystore2 is running without hardware backing, what actually happens to credential-backed keys?

When a VINTF manifest lies about StrongBox, which guarantees does the framework silently drop?

Three concrete observations on what a device in mid-bring-up state actually exposes

The failure modes during bring-up aren't random. They map directly to architectural decisions. Bring-up is the only context where you get to watch those decisions matter in real time - layer by layer, from nothing.

activities.title: One Language, All GPU: How Julia Targets different GPU backends from a Single Kernel.
activities.description:
GPU programming is usually synonymous with CUDA and with that comes vendor lock in, a steep learning curve, and code that only runs on NVIDIA hardware. In this talk, I'll share my experience as one of the maintainers of JuliaGPU, working on AcceleratedKernels.jl and GPUArrays.jl as part of Google Summer of Code, and show how Julia lets you write a single GPU kernel that runs unchanged on NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple GPUs.

We'll start from the ground up: what a GPU kernel actually is, why "write once, run on any GPU" matters for researchers and developers who don't want to be tied to one hardware vendor, and how KernelAbstractions.jl makes this possible through Julia's compiler infrastructure (GPUCompiler.jl, LLVM based codegen for multiple backends).

I'll walk through code snippets, a simple kernel, running it across backends, and then go deeper into how higher level operations are implemented across the JuliaGPU stack, the performance challenges involved (closing the gap with hand tuned libraries like PyTorch's kernels).Target Audience:

Developers curious about GPU programming.

Julia users wanting to use their GPUs without learning CUDA/HIP/etc.

Researchers in scientific computing, ML, or data science.

Open source contributors interested in compiler/runtime internals.

Anyone curious how a single high level language can target wildly different hardware.

FOSS Alignment:

JuliaGPU is a fully open source, community maintained ecosystem. This talk shares not just the technology but the experience of contributing to and maintaining a major open source project, encouraging attendees to get involved in GPU computing without needing access to expensive proprietary toolchains or vendor specific knowledge.
keyTakeaways: Rather than writing vendor specific kernel implementations, Julia kernel written with KernelAbstractions.jl can run on NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple GPUs without rewriting code.
Understand the layered structure of the JuliaGPU stack (GPUCompiler.jl → KernelAbstractions.jl → GPUArrays.jl/AcceleratedKernels.jl) and how each layer abstracts away vendor specific details.
Exposure to writing and running a GPU kernel, including how high level operations get compiled down to hardware specific code.

Insight into the performance engineering challenges of cross vendor GPU code where it lags hand tuned vendor libraries and what techniques (e.g. better memory access patterns, intrinsics, vectorised loads etc) help close the gap.
A look at what it's actually like to contribute to major open source GPU ecosystem, as motivation for attendees to get involved themselves.

activities.title: Keeping up with the AOSP
activities.description: The Android Open Source Project (AOSP) has undergone significant changes over the past year or so. Not just in new features, but also in how the project itself is developed and governed. This lightning talk provides a quick overview of the recent developments in the AOSP ecosystem, including the transition of AOSP main to read-only, introduction to android-latest-release branch, mandatory registration for app developers, the Android Automotive OS (AAOS) Software Defined Vehicle (SDV) release, updates from aosp-devs.org community and other updates shaping Android's future.

activities.title: Rust Is Not an HDL, So I Built a Tiny One.
activities.description:
Why hardware design and compiler development are more similar than they first appear.

My experience building a small HDL (Hardware Description Language) compiler in Rust.

Turning source code into hardware through parsing, ASTs, semantic analysis, and intermediate representations.

Challenges of thinking in hardware instead of software, including state, timing, and concurrency.

Design decisions, mistakes, and lessons learned while building the project.

How open-source projects such as LLVM, MLIR, CIRCT, Chisel, and RustHDL influenced the development process.

A live demonstration showing how a simple digital circuit moves through the compiler pipeline.

Practical takeaways for developers interested in compilers, systems programming, hardware tooling, and open-source development.
keyTakeaways: Understand how compiler concepts such as parsing, ASTs, semantic analysis, and code generation can be applied to hardware tooling.
Learn the key differences between software and hardware thinking, especially around state, timing, and concurrency.
See how a simple HDL compiler can be built using familiar systems programming techniques.
Gain insight into modern open-source hardware ecosystems and the tools that power them.
Walk away with practical ideas and resources for exploring compilers, hardware design, and language development projects of your own.

activities.title: What's new at FOSS United Foundation
Adapting Generic Boot Loader on Android platforms
activities.description:
Bootloaders are an essential block for booting an Android device. They handle tasks from reading the partitions, loading, and authenticating the Android images to preparing the board and finally handing over thec ontrol to kernel. Currently each vendor maintains different bootloader. To address the issue of fragmentation in the Android bootloader implementation across the community, Generic BootLoader (GBL) was introduced by Google.

GBL is an EFI application which supports x86, ARM64 and RISC-V architectures and can be run across various firmware such as U-Boot, EDK2, and LittleKernel. By leveraging RUST memory safety and trusted components such as libufdt and libavb, GBL provides a uniform, secure, and robust environment.

This session provides a technical breakdown into GBL’s integration within the UEFI ecosystem. We will explore how GBL utilizes standard upstream protocols and interfaces with firmware to select platform-appropriate Device Trees, apply essential DT fixups, and prepare critical data for the Android kernel, including bootconfig and command-line parameters. Overall, the session provides a practical look at the enhancements required to bring GBL into the boot chain along with the challenges that might be encountered, offering a comprehensive roadmap for developers looking to reduce maintenance overhead and accelerate future-ready Android deployments.

activities.title: Formal Verification: An Introduction through Elementary Arithmetic
activities.description: Formal verification is often viewed as a highly specialized area accessible only to seasoned developers and researchers. Yet the core idea - verifying that an implementation satisfies a particular specification - can be introduced very naturally and easily via the basic arithmetic algorithms one learns in school.In this talk I present a Lean 4 project that implements and proves the correctness of elementary pen-and-paper arithmetic algorithms, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, square-roots, and divisibility tests. Alongside the formal proofs, the project includes interactive visualizations that connect each step of an algorithm with the invariant or proof idea that justifies it. These visualizations allow users to follow both the execution of an algorithm and the invariants that justify its correctness.The main purpose of the talk is to make formal verification more approachable using basic algorithms everyone already knows very well. Using these algorithms as case studies, the talk demonstrates how correctness invariants arise naturally from the mathematical structure of an algorithm and how inductive reasoning can be translated into machine-checked proofs in Lean.
keyTakeaways: An accessible introduction to formal verification through familiar arithmetic algorithms.
An understanding of how theorem-proving concepts such as induction and invariants arise naturally when reasoning about algorithm correctness
An overview of how Lean 4 can be used to specify algorithms and construct machine-checked correctness proofs.
An appreciation for how interactive visualizations can make formal verification and theorem-proving concepts more approachable.

activities.title: Porting AOSP to Allwinner Sunxi platform
activities.description:
With our recent efforts to get upstream Linux Kernel support for Allwinner Sunxi A133 and A523 platforms, this also includes the Display Engine. Although the whole upstream effort relies on reverse engineering the vendor blobs, we have managed to get the end-to-end display pipeline working with GPU and got LVDS and MIPI working. In some cases, we are able to get 2 parallel displays working.

Allwinner ships the most affordable SoCs / silicons for gaming consoles and handheld devices including tablets, all running vendor-provided Android. All of the devices come with closed source and proprietary blobs from Imagination Technologies, ARM Mali, and CedarX for the media pipelines.

This talk walks through our adventurous journey in building AOSP with upstream Linux Kernel 7.1 without any vendor-provided components to run an end-to-end display pipeline. Don't Model Every Leaf: The Magic of Blender Geometry Nodes
activities.description:
After I learned enough parts of the basics of Blender, I was left with a question: "Man, if I had to build a huge scene, does it mean I have to model every leaf, every rock, every branch???"

I was convinced that pro Blender users surely knew a better way. I looked around for what that might be. That's when I discovered upon Geometry Nodes.

At first it came off as complex. It felt like I should have a PhD in Vector Math to understand what it does. But soon, I started to really get a hang of it and enjoy it. At its core, Geometry Nodes is a fancy name for flow chart. Its a node-based tool set used for procedural modeling, animation, and scene generation. Its a way to put together a factory for manufacturing 3D art within Blender. It is what I now spend most of my time on, and its truly magical.

In this talk, we’re skipping the dry, overwhelming math and focusing on the magic. We will look at how Geometry Nodes can radically speed up your workflow, unlock happy accidents, and bring back the sheer joy of experimentation. I’ll share what Geometry Nodes is actually capable of, break down a few fun examples I’ve created, and if time permits we'll do a quick walk through on how to build a setup that instantly generates Minecraft-style terrain.

If you have tinkered around with Blender a bit, even if you have not clicked on the "New Node Tree"; or you are an experienced artist; this talk is for you.

If you have never heard of Blender, but have heard of Minecraft, you might still enjoy it!
keyTakeaways: Whats a Node?: An almost beginner-friendly look at what procedural art actually means.
Real-World Examples: A showcase of fun, practical projects built with nodes (and why they were so fun to make).
Live Build: Minecraft-style terrain generator.

activities.title: How exactly can we teach students the right FOSS etiquette?
activities.description:
Every online tutorial and blog on “how to contribute to OSS” or “how to make your first PR” teaches the mechanics and commands, but almost none teach the etiquette: when it's okay to ping a maintainer, how to take a rejected proposal gracefully, why a half-finished AI-generated PR adds to stress and overload for the maintainers. Now that open source sits on the student resume(s) right next to internships and projects, this missing gap of education has real consequences: maintainers across GSoC, LFX and Hacktoberfest have publicly described waves of low-effort and spam contributions, with many OSS projects shutting down for new contributions.

This talk is about the cultural layer underneath a pipeline: the norms that decide whether a student community produces thoughtful contributors or AI spammers. A pipeline tells you how to get more students contributing; it says nothing about whether those contributions are any good for the projects on the receiving end.

At Point Blank, an OSS community we have been running for the last 7 years, we've spent the last few years turning that culture into something teachable, and we’ll walk through what actually worked:

A peer proposal-review gate : our "war rooms" so that of the ~40 GSoC proposals our members write in a season, none reach a maintainer as unreviewed slop. Every draft is torn apart by people who've been selected before it goes anywhere near an org.

A "contribute before you apply" norm, anchored by a Hacktoberfest kickoff and weekly sync-ups, so contribution is a sustained relationship with a project rather than a March résumé sprint.

An explicit etiquette curriculum covering what contributing.md leaves out: how to ask for help in public without spamming, how to treat a maintainer's time as the scarcest resource in the project, and how to behave when your contributions are rejected.

A mentor-handoff model: every contributor who gets selected comes back to coach the next batch, so etiquette is transmitted by example, not preached from a slide.

We will be honest about what didn't work, and about the awkward cases, including what we do with the member who openly just wants the T-shirt. We will close with a short, concrete checklist that maintainers and student-club organizers can adopt to keep their contribution spaces both welcoming to newcomers and resistant to spam.
keyTakeaways: A repeatable way to teach contribution etiquette, not just mechanics and why that distinction matters more in a hyper-competitive student culture.
A concrete proposal-review process that cuts low-effort and spam submissions at the source, including the trade-offs of running it at scale.
How to coach contributors through rejection so they stay civil and keep contributing.
A short checklist maintainers can use to set norms that invite newcomers without inviting spam.

activities.title: Property-based testing for UIs
activities.description:
How do you catch bugs that only show up when a user taps frantically, or when async data loads in an unexpected order? Standard UI tests miss this subtle stuff, even though it happens constantly in real, stateful applications.

In this talk we explore how to apply generative testing to the messy world of user interfaces. Property-based testing (PBT) autonomously explores an app using an actions generator and validates correctness properties at every step, which surfaces harder bugs earlier.

This talk answers:

I'll share how I built Sanderling, an open-source PBT framework for mobile and web apps. Testers define behavioral properties of the app in a simple TypeScript spec, then run the app against that spec in CI for hours to find property violations.

Why Now?

The number of things we ship is skyrocketing due to AI, and bugs too. Unit tests don't test user behavior, and integration tests mostly cover the happy path.

The state space of actions a user can execute in an app is huge and largely unexplored by example-based tests. If we test behavioral properties instead of specific business logic, an actions generator can drive the app through far more of that space than any example tests.

Overall, Compute is cheaper than ever. We need a system that runs for hours and tells us the app has a race condition when a user taps a button twice.
keyTakeaways: How property-based testing finds unexpected UI bugs that example-based tests can't
A case study of writing behavioral properties for an app and running them in a live environment
You don't need to be a formal-methods expert to get value from this. Simple properties uncover deep bugs, like ensuring a loading spinner eventually disappears, or that the screen never goes blank.

activities.title: When NO_PROXY Lies: Finding an IPv4-Mapped IPv6 Patch Bypass in Axios
activities.description:
In this talk, I’ll walk through how I analyzed a security fix in Axios and found that the patch still left a bypass route open through IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses. The original issue had already taught Axios to normalize some hostname edge cases for NO_PROXY, but the fix still relied on string comparisons after partial normalization. That left a gap where the same host could be represented differently enough to evade policy checks.

I’ll show how this happens in practice, why the Node/WHATWG URL stack turns mapped addresses into canonical IPv6 forms, and how that breaks exact NO_PROXY matching in a way that is easy to miss during patch review. The session will include a small, reproducible demo using a local proxy and a safe local target, and then walk through the remediation strategy to properly close the issue.

This is a case study in patch-bypass hunting for open-source software, reviewing a fix, reasoning about representation mismatches, and turning a tiny edge case into a maintainable engineering lesson for security-sensitive code.

The GHSA I reported has been accepted and fixed in the latest Axios. GitHub has issued CVE-2026-44492.

Ref. link: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pjwm-pj3p-43mv
keyTakeaways: How NO_PROXY, URL parsing, and host canonicalization interact in Node.js applications
Why IPv4-mapped IPv6 is a practical security problem and not just a formatting oddity
A repeatable methodology for finding patch bypasses by reviewing what a fix normalized and what it still compared as raw text
Concrete lessons maintainers can apply when enforcing network policy in OSS libraries

activities.title: Can We Build a Copyleft License for Community Data in the Age of AI
activities.description:
As community-generated datasets become increasingly important for training AI systems, there is a growing need to explore whether existing open data licenses adequately protect community contributions. This session will examine whether copyleft principles, which have successfully supported open source software ecosystems, can be adapted to datasets used for AI development. The discussion will focus on attribution, reciprocity, data provenance, community ownership, and the governance of data commons.

Community-led initiatives across India and the world are creating datasets that support language technologies, accessibility tools, and AI research. However, many of these datasets are released without licensing frameworks specifically designed for AI use. This creates a risk that community-generated data may be incorporated into proprietary AI systems without attribution, transparency, or any meaningful contribution back to the communities that created them. Open source software have relied on copyleft licenses such as the GNU GPL to ensure that software and improvements remain available to the community. As community-generated datasets become increasingly important for training AI systems, a similar question is emerging for data i.e. can copyleft principles and licence be applied to datasets used for machine learning?

A draft Community Data License has been developed by Viswam.ai and SFLC.in to address these concerns by applying copyleft principles to datasets. The proposed license seeks to ensure that community-generated datasets remain part of a shared commons by requiring attribution to original contributors, transparency regarding data provenance, and the sharing of modified or derived datasets under the same licence terms.

This session will use the draft license as a starting point for a broader discussion on the future of community data governance, open AI, and digital commons. The objective is to gather perspectives from developers, researchers, open-source contributors, civil society organisations, policymakers, and dataset creators on whether new licensing and governance approaches are needed to protect community data commons and how such a license could work in practice.

Open discussion with participants. The session will begin with a brief introduction to the problem statement and the draft Community Data License, followed by a moderated discussion. Participants will be encouraged to share experiences, concerns, use cases, and perspectives from technical, legal, policy, research, and community viewpoints. The moderator will guide the discussion around key questions and explore broad conversation focused on the topic.

activities.title: Shaili Sanchaya: Reviving Indic Typography from Archival Metadata
activities.description:
While the digital ecosystem for Latin scripts thrives with thousands of open-source typefaces, Indic typography - particularly for languages such as Kannada - remains severely underrepresented. Most contemporary Indic fonts are designed for modern publishing and do not preserve the historical letterforms, ligatures, and typographic variations found in nineteenth- and early twentieth-century print traditions.

At Sanchaya (Sanchaya.org), we are exploring how the extensive digital archives created through the Servants of Knowledge initiative can help revive early print heritage. We have developed Shaili Sanchaya, an open-source toolchain for revival font development that extracts historical glyphs and letterforms from scanned public-domain books and pre-computer-era print collections to create modern, standards-compliant Unicode typefaces.

Beyond preserving typographic heritage, revival fonts are essential for improving OCR accuracy on historical documents. By digitally recreating legacy typefaces, we enable better recognition of older publications and help unlock vast collections of Indic knowledge that remain inaccessible to search, research, and dissemination.

We will present our open-source workflow - from archival scanning and character extraction to glyph normalization, vectorization, and font engineering—and discuss the challenges of revival font development, as well as how such efforts can lay the foundation for large-scale Indic glyph datasets and future machine learning applications.
keyTakeaways: The Indic Typography Gap: The lay man’s understanding the design and technical constraints of digital Indic typefaces.
Archival to Digital Pipeline: How to leverage community-digitized public archives (like Servants of Knowledge) for historical font revival.
FOSS Font Engineering: Talk about open-source tools? or tell the story of what help was out there to start thinking about unicode-compliant Indic fonts.
The Bigger Picture: How opening up glyph datasets can revolutionize OCR, archival indexing, and accessibility across regional Indic languages

activities.title: Surviving as an Open Source Startup : Xeneva
activities.description:
At IndiaFOSS 2025, we made our public debut. Back then, Xeneva was mostly in the wannabe startup stage, trying to build an operating system completely from scratch while balancing college. Since then, a lot has happened. We got backed by Zerodha's grant, exhibited at MangaloreFOSS, took our prototype to AWE Asia in Singapore, and engaged with multiple industry professionals to take our project forward. Ultimately, we managed to build a small team, gave up everything else, and are shifting to Bangalore to pursue this full-time.

This talk is a reality check on what happens after the initial hype. Building an independent, indigenous OS is... not really an easy task. Plus, we had to get into a niche to begin with. After careful research, we got into XR/AR/VR. But building it as an open-source startup, especially in the XR and smart glasses space where companies usually lock down their ecosystems, is kind of a different approach.

Xeneva actually started six years ago, and for the first five, it was more of a hobby. We want to share the unfiltered experience of making that jump from a 5 year old side project to a full time deep-tech startup. Specifically, we want to talk about this at IndiaFOSS because this time last year, we were at IndiaFOSS, and this event is what helped us make the transition. We’ll talk about why we actively chose to remain open-source when going closed might seem like the obvious route for an XR Startup whose main USP is its IP.

Most importantly, we want to highlight the beauty of open source and how we are only still here because we are open-source. The community support, the early equity-free grant, and the sheer visibility of building in the open are the exact reasons a project like Xeneva could survive.
keyTakeaways: The actual feasibility of running an open-source deep tech startup (and keeping the lights on).
Why we chose to be open-source & the strategic advantage of FOSS even when one could easily choose to remain closed.
The Community Lifeline: How we are literally only here today because we chose the open-source route.
Transitioning from a hobby-project to running a startup full-time.
Devoting our early career to FOSS.
Navigating funds without compromising our principle.

activities.title: Seqout: search engine for the world’s genomic data
activities.description:
DNA is the molecular blueprint of life. Modern sequencing technologies allow us to read DNA and RNA at unprecedented scale, generating vast amounts of biological data from organisms, tissues, and individual cells. Today, public repositories host millions of sequencing experiments comprising petabytes of data that power discoveries in medicine, drug development, agriculture, and fundamental biology.

Yet finding the right dataset is often harder than analysing it. Researchers must navigate fragmented repositories, heterogeneous metadata standards, and incomplete descriptions, making dataset discovery a time-consuming and frustrating process. With Seqout (https://seqout.org), we set out to build a genomics search engine that is fast, comprehensive, and lean enough to run on modest hardware while serving hundreds of thousands of researchers worldwide. Seqout is built entirely on open-source software: PostgreSQL and Neo4j power keyword and graph-based search, while embedding-based retrieval is enabled by open-source models and libraries from Hugging Face.

In this talk, we will discuss the engineering challenges involved in building a low-latency search engine over millions of biological datasets with limited resources (aka compute and GPUs). We will cover data ingestion, metadata normalisation, indexing strategies, typo tolerance, semantic search, and the trade-offs involved in integrating relational and graph databases with vector search.

Along the way, we'll share lessons learned from operating search infrastructure at scale and discuss how open-source software powers every layer of the platform. We'll also discuss how Seqout's MCP server enables large language models and AI agents to move beyond answering biology questions to directly discover and interact with relevant scientific datasets.
keyTakeaways: How to build a low-latency search engine from scratch
Combining PostgreSQL, Neo4j, and semantic search to improve dataset discovery
Lessons learned from building and operating an open-source scientific search platform

activities.title: OpenTCAD: A FOSS Python Pipeline for Semiconductor Process and Device Simulation
activities.description:
Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools span three levels - ones at the PCB design level, at the chip design level and at its most physics-heavy, at the transistor level. We have excellent FOSS tools at the PCB design level (KiCAD, tscircuit) and chip design level (OpenROAD, KLayout) but relatively little at the layer underneath : TCAD, the physics-heavy simulations of how transistors with a particular stack are fabricated and how they behave. Almost all of the existing tools are proprietary - Synopsys Sentaurus and Silvaco Atlas dominate, with licenses costing thousands of dollars per bench.

OpenTCAD is an attempt to close that gap. It is a modular Python framework that stitches together best-in-class FOSS components: Gmsh for meshing, ViennaPS for process topography, FiPy for doping diffusion, DEVSIM for drift-diffusion device simulation, into a single unified pipeline: process recipe → meshed structure with doping → device I-V characteristics. This involves bridging different libraries, defining a common mesh data format that carries material, doping and contact information in between different modules.

This talk discusses why TCAD matters, why the existing FOSS pieces have not been glued together before, the architecture choices made while building OpenTCAD, and a live demo simulating a device from a process recipe to an I-V curve.
keyTakeaways: What TCAD is, how it sits below chip-design in the EDA stack at the fab level, and why the FOSS ecosystem has a gap here
A tour of the mature FOSS components (Gmsh, ViennaPS, DEVSIM, FiPy) that already exist in isolation
How OpenTCAD's MeshField data model carries physics-meaningful values across process/device boundaries
A working demo: process recipe in, I-V curve out, all in Python
How to contribute: calibration data, device models, and process steps are all areas where the project needs help

activities.title: Extending Capa for Malicious Script Analysis
activities.description:
Malware analysis is essential for understanding the behaviour of malicious software. While tools like capa can identify capabilities in native executables, extending similar analysis to scripts such as Python, Bash, JavaScript and C# broadens its support beyond binaries.

Capa is an open-source malware analysis tool that identifies the capabilities of executable files, including PE, ELF, .NET module, shellcode and sandbox reports. It extracts low-level features from the input like API calls, strings and instruction sequence, matches them against the capa-rules and reports the detected behaviours in a structured format.

This talk is about my Google Summer of Code project with FLARE organization where I am integrating a new feature in the capa tool. Currently, capa supports the analysis of the executable files and sandbox reports. My work extends capa to support analysis of scripting languages such as Python, Bash, JavaScript and C# using Tree-Sitter library. Tree-Sitter is an open source parser generator library which builds concrete syntax trees of the source file to extract language-specific features.

The talk will begin with a brief introduction of my journey into open source and Google Summer of Code. I will then explain capa's architecture and capability analysis workflow, followed by the design and implementation of the Tree-sitter integration. The session will cover the architectural decisions behind the implementation and how Tree-sitter enables capability extraction from scripting languages.

The talk will conclude with a live demonstration of capa's binary analysis along with the newly added script analysis support. By the end of the session, attendees will understand capa's architecture, its analysis workflow and the benefits of extending it with scripting language support.
keyTakeaways: Understand how capa identifies the capabilities of malware.
Learn how Tree-sitter enables analysis of scripting languages in capa.
Explore the architecture of capa and integration of the Tree-sitter library.
See a live demonstration of binary and script analysis in capa.

activities.title: Computationalizing landscapes: The CoRE stack data structure for social-ecological diagnostics and planning
activities.description: The CoRE Stack (Commoning for Resilience and Equality) is a community-based digital public infrastructure consisting of datasets, algorithm pipelines, and user-facing tools, that can be used by rural communities and other stakeholders to improve the sustainability and resilience of their local landscapes. It brings together over a hundred variables (and growing) to describe landscape units like micro-watersheds in terms of changes in the area over the years in cropping intensity, water-table levels, health of waterbodies, forests and plantations, and welfare fund allocation, among others, sourced from multiple contributors or built using open ML models operating on satellite data. The unique aspect with the CoRE stack is that all this is assembled in a neat entity-relation data structure which describes landscapes in terms of discrete spatial units with nesting, intersection, and other relationships between them. This makes it computationally accessible to slice and dice the data like we would in a data frame, to understand landscapes more closely. We will present this data structure and the remarkable agility it unlocks in building new applications on top of it. We will demonstrate this through a novel application, CoRE insights, which uses the CoRE stack data on the one side, and extracts landscape diagnostic rulesets using LLMs from research papers on the other side, to build a neurosymbolic framework that can apply these rulesets to diagnose specific problems in a landscape, like whether or not it is suffering from groundwater stress, or rainfed agricultural risk, and so on, with uncertainty information on this determination. Another layer, the CoRE lens, is a library we are developing to interact with the data more easily using a functional programming approach which keeps the code short and easy to debug and understand. We will conclude with real stories of change on the ground using the CoRE stack, where the tools are in use by landscape stewards in 1500+ villages in India to build water security and ecological restoration plans with communities.
